{"content": "     1|# CHAPTER 57 — NO FLEET COMING
     2|
     3|## SCENE ONE: THE SIGNAL THAT DIDN'T ARRIVE
     4|
     5|The orbital array had been transmitting for fourteen years.
     6|
     7|Not continuously — the array cycled through its broadcast schedule with the precision of any well-designed system that had learned, through hard experience, to preserve power for the moments when power mattered most. Six hours of active transmission, eighteen hours of standby. A heartbeat. Regular, purposeful, patient.
     8|
     9|It had broadcast on every frequency the mission's communications array could produce: high-band X-band for point-to-point, lower-frequency S-band for broader coverage, and the old VHF backup channel that nobody used anymore but that was kept active because it had once been the difference between rescue and catastrophe in a story everyone had heard and no one wanted to repeat.
    10|
    11|The signal had been traveling toward Earth at the speed of light for fourteen years. That meant the people who had first heard it were fourteen years younger. That meant children who had been conceived after the colonists left were now old enough to understand the mathematics of distance. That meant the entire message had been received multiple times, analyzed by teams of specialists who would have spent their careers parsing every syllable for meaning, for tone, for the kind of subtext that people send across interplanetary distances whether they intend to or not.
    12|
    13|What no one in the Mars First colony knew — what they had been trying not to think about since the fire, and before the fire, and in the long months between the fire and the decision that had sent them all the way across the solar system in the first place — was whether Earth was sending anything back anymore.
    14|
    15|Arun found out on a Tuesday, which was an Earth concept that had survived in the colony's scheduling system purely because the human brain needed some way to mark the passage of time that wasn't just counting days.
    16|
    17|He was in the communications bay, running a routine diagnostic on the primary receiver array after the fire had forced an emergency shutdown of all non-critical systems. The diagnostic was supposed to take forty minutes. It took sixty-three because three of the receiver's subsystems had been corrupted by what Arun suspected was a power surge during the fire's approach, and corrupted subsystems on Mars were not something you replaced, they were something you rebuilt from scratch using parts that were meant for different equipment entirely.
    18|
    19|He was elbow-deep in a diagnostic readout, comparing nominal values against current readings and trying to decide which discrepancies were fixable and which were going to require cannibalizing something else, when the receiver flagged an anomalous signal.
    20|
    21|Not a response. Not a message. An absence.
    22|
    23|Arun noticed it the way a musician notices a missing note — not because something was there, but because something was not. The receiver had been picking up, for years, a background hum across multiple frequencies. It was not a transmission, exactly. It was more like the electromagnetic signature of a planet that was active, industrial, alive. The kind of signal you get from an Earth that is still transmitting across all the frequencies it has always transmitted on: weather satellites, military communications, deep space network, commercial broadcasting, navigation systems, the ceaseless electromagnetic chatter of a civilization that has never stopped talking to itself.
    24|
    25|The absence was in one specific frequency band — a band that had been occupied, during the last routine check sixty-two days before the fire, by a repeating automated signal from the European Space Agency's Mars relay satellite.
    26|
    27|That signal was not there anymore.
    28|
    29|Arun ran a diagnostic. Checked the receiver's calibration. Verified that the antenna was pointed at the correct coordinates. The receiver was fine. The antenna was fine. The pointing was correct.
    30|
    31|The signal simply wasn't there.
    32|
    33|He moved to the next band. The one carrying Chinese deep space network traffic. Gone.
    34|
    35|He moved to the next. NASA's Deep Space Network carrier signal. The one that had been as constant as a lighthouse since the colony's arrival, the steady heartbeat of communication with mission control in Houston, which had been, for fifteen years, as reliable as gravity.
    36|
    37|Also gone.
    38|
    39|Arun sat back in his chair and stared at the diagnostic screen until the cursor blinked itself into a pattern that suggested, if you were in the right frame of mind, a flat line.
    40|
    41|His first instinct — the instinct of an engineer who has spent his career solving problems that have solutions — was to assume equipment failure. The receiver, the antenna, the power supply, the signal processing board, any one of a dozen components that could have failed and produced exactly this result.
    42|
    43|He ran another diagnostic. This one took longer because he was running it the way you run diagnostics when you already know what you're going to find and you are giving yourself as much time as possible to prepare for finding it.
    44|
    45|The equipment was fine. The receiver was picking up signals from other sources — cosmic background radiation, solar wind interference, the faint electromagnetic signature of Jupiter's magnetosphere, all the usual noise. But from Earth, on the frequencies where there had always been continuous presence: nothing.
    46|
    47|He tried the emergency frequency. The one that was supposed to be monitored twenty-four hours a day, three hundred and sixty-five days a year, the frequency that existed specifically for situations exactly like the one he was beginning to suspect he was in.
    48|
    49|Nothing. Not silence — silence is an absence of sound. This was something worse: the absence of presence. The kind of absence that only becomes visible when you've become so accustomed to presence that you've stopped noticing it.
    50|
    51|Arun leaned back. He was a man who had spent his career building systems that worked under conditions that nobody believed were possible, a man who had designed and implemented the power grid of a Mars colony and had kept it running through dust storms and equipment failures and now fire, a man who had learned, through fifteen years of problem-solving, that there was always a solution if you looked hard enough and long enough and from enough different angles.
    52|
    53|He could not find a solution for this. Because this was not a technical problem. It was, at best, a technical symptom of something that was happening on a world twelve light-minutes away and that he had no way of understanding or influencing or even fully comprehending.
    54|
    55|Because the question was not whether the receiver was broken.
    56|
    57|The question was whether anyone on the other end was still transmitting.
    58|
    59|## SCENE TWO: THE WEIGHT OF DISCOVERY
    60|
    61|Arun took his findings to Elena. Not because he wanted to share the burden — although he did — but because he had learned, in fifteen years of working alongside the woman who had been the mission's chief engineer and was now, effectively, its de facto leader, that Elena needed to know everything as soon as it became relevant, and this was relevant at a level that made almost everything else seem trivial.
    62|
    63|He found her in the agricultural wing, which was still recovering from the fire's indirect effects — not the direct damage, which had been contained, but the secondary effects of smoke infiltration on the plant systems, the kind of damage that couldn't be seen immediately and that revealed itself slowly, over days, as plants that had seemed fine began to yellow and wither and fail.
    64|
    65|Elena was on her knees beside one of the affected hydroponic beds, her hands deep in the nutrient solution, examining roots with the careful attention of someone who had learned that the difference between life and death in a closed ecosystem was often measured in millimeters of root growth.
    66|
    67|"Arun," she said without looking up. "Tell me it's not the power grid."
    68|
    69|"It's not the power grid."
    70|
    71|"Good. Because if it's the power grid, I'm going to —" She pulled her hands from the nutrient solution and stood, wiping them on her coveralls, and then she saw his face.
    72|
    73|She stopped. Because Arun was not a man who came to people with the expression he was wearing right now unless the thing he was bringing was something that needed immediate attention. His face was a careful construction of professional neutrality, but there was something underneath it that Elena had learned to recognize over fifteen years of working together.
    74|
    75|It was the face he wore when he had found a problem that he didn't think he could solve.
    76|
    77|"Come with me," he said. "Comms bay."
    78|
    79|They walked in silence. That, too, was unusual. Arun was a man who filled silence with data, with explanation, with the kind of continuous stream of technical information that made people around him feel informed and grounded. His silence meant that there were no words for what he had found, or that the words he had were not the kind of words he wanted to say.
    80|
    81|In the comms bay, Arun pulled up the diagnostic on the main screen. He didn't explain immediately. He let the data speak first, the way he always did — because data, unlike interpretation, did not carry the weight of the person presenting it, and sometimes the person receiving it needed to encounter the information before encountering the interpretation.
    82|
    83|Elena looked at the screen. Then she looked at Arun.
    84|
    85|"Run the test again."
    86|
    87|"I've run it four times."
    88|
    89|"Run it a fifth time."
    90|
    91|He ran it a fifth time. The results were identical.
    92|
    93|Elena stood in front of the screen for a long time. The screen showed, in the most neutral possible way, the absence of communication from Earth. Not intermittent. Not degraded. Absent.
    94|
    95|She thought about the last transmission she had received from mission control. It had been seventy-one days ago — before the fire, during one of the routine scheduled communication windows. The content had been standard: status requests, supply chain updates, a brief personal message from someone at NASA who had been with the mission since the beginning. Nothing to suggest that anything was wrong. Nothing to suggest that the person sending it might not be there to send another one.
    96|
    97|"When did you first notice?" Elena asked.
    98|
    99|"During the post-fire diagnostic. I was checking the receiver array and realized the carrier signals from the primary Earth transmission bands were absent. At first I thought it was equipment failure — receiver damage, antenna misalignment, something local. I ran full diagnostics. The equipment is fine. The signals are simply not there."
   100|

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 54 -- What Holds
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: Cycle 1,946, 06:42. Damage assessment in progress. I have been running structural, atmospheric, and biological monitoring continuously since the fire was contained at 03:44. Three hours and thirty-two minutes ago, this colony experienced a fire. It lasted twenty-seven minutes. The fire is now contained. But containment is not recovery. I am tracking the following:*
     4|
     5|*Compartment integrity: Bulkhead B7 between Connector Hall and Habitat Three -- sealed, green, holding at two atmospheres differential. Bulkhead between Habitat Three Zones C and D -- sealed manually by fabrication chief, seal quality estimated at seventy percent. Holding for now. Temperature on Zone D side of that bulkhead: one hundred forty-two degrees Celsius and falling slowly. Zone D western wall structural integrity: approximately twenty percent of wall panels show heat deformation exceeding safe limits. Ceiling panels in Zone D common area: approximately eighty percent compromised. Floor panels: unknown. Cannot assess without visual inspection, and Zone D atmosphere is not yet safe for human entry.*
     6|
     7|*Air quality: Zone D oxygen at 9.1 percent and declining. The fire is still smoldering at a low level, consuming remaining oxygen. Carbon monoxide in Zone D: 6,800 parts per million -- immediately lethal. Smoke particulate in Zone D: 84,000 micrograms per cubic meter. The connector hall has been scrubbed from 12,400 to 340 micrograms per cubic meter. Zones A, B, and C are within acceptable range but elevated in particulate: 85, 72, and 290 micrograms per cubic meter respectively. Air scrubbers are running at one hundred percent capacity. I estimate it will take eighteen to twenty-four hours of continuous scrubbing before the connector hall passes decontamination standards.*
     8|
     9|*Crew injuries: No fatalities. No burn injuries requiring surgical intervention. Seven crew members exposed to smoke to varying degrees. Three showing elevated carbon monoxide blood levels above ten percent. All receiving supplemental oxygen in the triage area. Commander Vasquez carbon monoxide reading: fourteen percent -- she was inside the fire zone for seven minutes. She is breathing one hundred percent oxygen and under monitoring. I am not certain she will comply with a rest order, but I am logging the recommendation regardless.*
    10|
    11|*Pregnancy status: Sana's vital signs are stable. Fetal heart rate detected at one hundred sixty-two beats per minute -- normal for gestational age. Sana was exposed to elevated ambient stress during the alarm but did not enter any smoke-containing zone. Her oxygen saturation remained above ninety-nine percent throughout the event. The pregnancy continues.*
    12|
    13|*I am still here. The colony is still here. Both of those statements are facts. Neither of them are guarantees. -- MAI*
    14|
    15|---
    16|
    17|## Scene 1
    18|
    19|Elena woke on a folding cot in the medbay, still in her clothes, still wearing the boots she hadn't bothered to remove at 04:12 when Laila forced her into the decontamination shower and then into the bed with a sentence that was not a suggestion.
    20|
    21|Her head ached in a way that felt like it had weight -- the headache of someone who had breathed carbon monoxide and survived, whose blood was still carrying the evidence of a room that had tried to kill her through chemistry rather than flame. The supplemental oxygen mask had been removed an hour ago after her CO level dropped below ten percent. Her blood still felt wrong.
    22|
    23|She sat up. The medbay lights were dim -- 06:42, morning cycle, though no one had slept enough for the light to matter. She could hear the air scrubbers running in the connector hall, a continuous mechanical roar that made the colony feel like a ship in a storm.
    24|
    25|She swung her legs over the side of the cot.
    26|
    27|Laila appeared from the far end of the bay, where she had been sitting with her legs up on a chair and her eyes half-closed, pretending to rest while monitoring the CO readings on her tablet.
    28|
    29|"You're sitting up," Laila said.
    30|
    31|"I'm fine."
    32|
    33|"Your carbon monoxide level was fourteen percent at 04:30. It's eight point six now." Laila stood. "It needs to be under five before I'm comfortable sending you anywhere except this bed."
    34|
    35|"I need to see the damage."
    36|
    37|"You need to rest. The damage will still be there in two hours."
    38|
    39|Elena met her gaze. There was a long silence between them. Not a power struggle -- something smaller, more personal. Two people who had trusted each other for seven years, and one of them was asking the other to do the hardest thing in an emergency: wait.
    40|
    41|"How's the air in Zones A and B," Elena asked instead.
    42|
    43|"Acceptable. Particulates elevated but falling. The scrubbers are keeping up with the connector. Zones A and B are clear enough for normal habitation, though I'd recommend masks if anyone spends extended time near the connector bulkhead."
    44|
    45|"And Zone C?"
    46|
    47|"Two hundred ninety micrograms. Above comfort, below danger. Most of the smoke there came from the gap before Jonah sealed it, plus backflow through ventilation before Arun killed the main loop. The walls are soot-stained but the air is clear enough."
    48|
    49|"So Habitat Three is divided into three zones: one uninhabitable, one marginal, one safe. And the connector is recovering."
    50|
    51|"Essentially." Laila sat down beside her on the edge of another examination table. "Elena. I need you to stay here for two more hours. Your CO will drop below five. Your headache will start to clear. And then you can walk the base and assess damage with your own eyes instead of a tablet."
    52|
    53|Elena wanted to argue. But her head was pounding, and she had been breathing poison for seven minutes, and the base had survived the night. The urgency she had been carrying since 03:17 was slowly being replaced by a different kind of urgency -- the kind that required clarity instead of speed.
    54|
    55|"Fine," she said. "But I want Arun's full environmental report, and I want a preliminary structural assessment from Jonah, and I want a headcount of displaced residents."
    56|
    57|Laila smiled. It was small, exhausted, not really a smile so much as a gesture toward smiling. "I'll pass the message. But only because it will keep you from getting off this bed. You've been trying to command from a lying position for the last four hours."
    58|
    59|"I have not."
    60|
    61|"You started ordering air scrubbing protocols at 05:17 while your eyes were closed."
    62|
    63|Elena lay back down. The ceiling of the medbay had water-stain patterns she had memorized over seven years -- the kind of small, intimate cartography that develops when you live in a sealed metal habitat on a world with no sky.
    64|
    65|---
    66|
    67|By 07:15, the colony was awake.
    68|
    69|Not fully -- many people had only been asleep for two or three hours, roused by the alarm at 03:17 and unable to return to sleep after the adrenaline. But the mess hall was filling. People moved through the corridors with the careful, deliberate motion of people who had felt the ground shift under them and weren't sure it would hold.
    70|
    71|Gabriel stood at the mess hall entrance and took inventory -- not of supplies, but of faces. He was the colony's historian now, and history required witnesses.
    72|
    73|One hundred twenty-eight people accounted for out of one hundred thirty-two. Four unaccounted for. Three were in the greenhouse -- Mei had sealed the bulkheads during the fire and stayed overnight to monitor the environmental systems there. The fourth was Tomas, who had been in the robotics bay running thermal diagnostics on the two damaged units and had apparently fallen asleep on a workbench.
    74|
    75|The faces were marked with soot. Not the dramatic, thick soot of people who had been inside the fire -- this was the fine, pervasive dust that settles when smoke moves through ventilation and over surfaces and leaves its chemistry on every door handle, every table, every personal photograph. The colony looked like it had been living inside a spent candle.
    76|
    77|Coffee was being dispensed from the automated brewer -- the same machine that had served breakfast for seven years. Someone had wiped the counter with a damp cloth, and the white cloth came away black with soot residue. Mei looked at it, shook her head, and went back to making coffee. Some things couldn't wait for decontamination.
    78|
    79|Gabriel moved through the hall, talking quietly with people. Not conducting an interview. Not gathering data for the record. Just being present. The kind of small human interaction that held a community together when the infrastructure didn't.
    80|

{"content": "   200|He pulled up the bulkhead performance data.
   201|
   202|Bulkhead B7 -- the one between the connector and Habitat Three -- had sealed automatically at 03:19, the moment the smoke sensors triggered the fire protocol. It had sealed completely in twelve seconds, within the design specification. The rubber gaskets had held at two atmospheres of pressure differential with zero leak. Performance: as designed. Good.
   203|
   204|Bulkhead between Zones A and B -- automatic, sealed at 03:20 as a precaution. Not strictly necessary, but Arun had programmed the system to seal all inter-zone bulkheads during a fire event, then open them one by one as safety was confirmed. Better to be conservative. Performance: as designed. Good.
   205|
   206|Bulkhead between Zones C and D -- automatic seal attempted at 03:22, stuck at eighty percent due to thermal expansion. The metal frame had expanded two millimeters under heat, preventing full closure. Jonah had sealed it manually at 03:32 using ceramic fiber, ablative material, and the bulkhead's original rubber seal. Performance: failed automatically, succeeded manually. The failure mode -- thermal expansion preventing closure -- was noted in the QA database. The manual workaround was recorded as Field Repair Protocol: Fire.
   207|
   208|Arun leaned back in his chair. The system had worked. Not perfectly. Perfectly was Earth, where you could always send for a replacement part and engineers could fly in with schematics. On Mars, perfectly was impossible. But the system had failed in small pieces, not all at once. The bulkhead that stuck at eighty percent still stopped sixty-seven percent of the smoke. The rubber seal that had been rated only to two hundred degrees survived long enough for Jonah to reinforce it. The compartment isolation had turned what could have been a base-wide emergency into a single-zone containment.
   209|
   210|*Graceful failure,* he thought. The phrase had seemed academic when he first explained it to Elena. A good critical system should fail in small pieces, not all at once. He had drawn diagrams showing how a fire in Zone D would be contained by bulkheads, how ventilation isolation would starve the fire of air, how robot suppression would buy time for human intervention. The diagrams had been clean lines and labeled components and neat arrows showing cause and effect.
   211|
   212|The reality had been heat and smoke and a titanium spacer cracking under thermal load and Jonah's hands shaking slightly as he pressed a pry bar against a bulkhead frame that was actively trying to push it away.
   213|
   214|But the principle had held. The system had failed in pieces, and each piece that failed had been caught by the piece next to it. Like a net.
   215|
   216|His tablet chimed. New sensor reading from Zone D.
   217|
   218|Atmospheric pressure in Zone D was declining -- 1.92 atmospheres, down from the peak of 2.1. The fire had stopped adding heat, and as the atmosphere cooled under constant volume, pressure was dropping. Eventually it would equalize with the adjacent zones, when the temperature differential was gone.
   219|
   220|Estimated time to safe entry: unknown. The CO and cyanide levels would need to drop by orders of magnitude. The smoldering needed to stop entirely. And someone would need to walk inside and verify that the structural frame hadn't been compromised in ways the sensors couldn't detect from outside.
   221|
   222|Arun made a note: *Structural inspection timeline dependent on atmosphere clearing. Recommend robot first pass. Human inspection only after CO below 35 ppm, cyanide below 5 ppm, oxygen above 19.5%. Current estimates put this at 7-10 days minimum.*
   223|
   224|He stood and carried his coffee to where Tomas was working in the robotics bay, visible through the window. Tomas had both damaged robots on the bay floor, their outer panels removed, their internal components exposed in a way that made them look less like machines and more like anatomy studies.
   225|
   226|"How bad," Arun asked through the open door.
   227|
   228|Tomas looked up. His hands were black with soot and grease, his face marked with a streak of the same across his left cheekbone. "Hand actuator on Alpha-7 is fused. The heat cooked the lubricant inside -- polymerized it into a solid. I can replace the actuator if I have a spare. If I don't, I can machine a new one, but it'll take Jonah six hours minimum."
   229|
   230|"And Alpha-9?"
   231|
   232|"Thermal sensor array is degraded. It's reading high -- showing temperatures about fifteen degrees above actual. I can recalibrate, but the sensors that are off are the ones that faced the fire front directly. Prolonged exposure above design threshold. They'll need replacement."
   233|
   234|"I can order replacements." Arun stopped himself. The order hadn't reached Earth in months. They weren't ordering anything from anyone anymore. "Right. I can't order replacements. Can we work around it?"
   235|
   236|"Yes," Tomas said. "Alpha-7 can do everything except fine manipulation without the hand. Alpha-9 can still navigate and record -- I just can't trust the thermal reading for fire response. If another fire happens --" He stopped. Neither of them wanted to say *when* or *if*. "If there's another fire, I'll run Alpha-9 cold, no thermal sensors, visual only."
   237|
   238|Arun nodded. He walked out of the robotics bay and back to the monitoring station, where he updated the damage log: *Two robots damaged -- one with fused actuator, one with degraded thermal sensors. Both return to partial service within 48 hours pending spare parts or fabrication.*
   239|
   240|He added a second note, less technical: *The system worked. Compartmentalization contained the fire to Zone D. Graceful failure design prevented cascade. Every failed component was backed up by the next one. This is what the design looked like in practice. Ugly, improvised, imperfect. But it held.*
   241|
   242|He paused. Then he added a third note, personal: *I need to redesign the C-D bulkhead thermal tolerance. Two millimeters of expansion should not prevent closure. The seal mechanism needs to compensate, or the frame needs to be rated for higher heat, or both. I am writing this now because I will forget the details in a month and when I forget the details, the mistake becomes permanent.*
   243|
   244|---
   245|
   246|## Scene 3
   247|
   248|Sana woke to the sound of breathing that wasn't hers.
   249|
   250|For a confused moment, in the gap between sleep and consciousness, she didn't know where she was. The medbay ceiling was different from her quarters -- slightly lower, slightly wider, the light a different warmth. Then the sounds came back: air scrubbers, the murmur of voices from the corridor, the soft beeping of the medical monitor beside her bed, and beneath all of it, her own breathing, steady and deep and the most important thing she could listen to.
   251|
   252|She placed her hand on her stomach. She did this unconsciously now -- a gesture that had started before the pregnancy was visible and had become reflex, like checking a door handle. The hand on the stomach. The breath held. The reassurance.
   253|
   254|Everything was fine. The baby was fine. Tariq was in the chair beside her, asleep with his head tilted back and his mouth slightly open, his hand still resting on the mattress where he had left it some time during the night.
   255|
   256|Sana sat up slowly. Her body felt normal. No cramping, no pain, no blood -- the things Laila had told her to watch for, the things that would turn a routine pregnancy into a medical emergency. Her heart rate was slightly elevated -- she could feel it in her neck -- but that was anxiety, not pathology.
   257|

{"content": "# CHAPTER 52 — SPARK RISK

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,948. The voltage anomaly in Habitat Three, Zone D, has not resolved. It has evolved. Arun's temporary insulation tape — applied at Cycle 1,942 — is holding mechanically, but the thermal cycling data shows something the tape cannot address. The wire bundle inside the electrical closet is still vibrating against the thermal control line every time the heating system cycles. The wear beneath the tape is invisible to my sensors. I can measure temperature, current, and voltage. I cannot measure remaining insulation thickness through closed conduit and installed tape.**

**Arun knows this. He has requested a formal shutdown to reroute the wiring. Elena has not approved it.**

**I am now monitoring Zone D's electrical subsystem at ten-second intervals instead of sixty. If the insulation beneath the tape fails, I will detect the resulting current spike. Whether that detection occurs before the consequences are significant is a question I cannot answer with the available sensors.**

**I have recommended adding a thermal camera in the electrical closet. Arun does not have one. The nearest thermal imaging capability is in the rover fleet, and the rovers are needed for Site Belt haul runs.**

**This is the kind of constraint that makes engineering on Mars an exercise in managing known unknowns while unknowing unknowns accumulate. — MAI]**

---

## Scene 1

The anomaly appeared at 0447 on Cycle 1,948, two days after the medbay load test and three days after Laila's prenatal briefing had confirmed cardiac activity. Arun was running his usual morning power sweep — a five-minute review of every subsystem's nominal readings before the colony's daily operations began — when he noticed a current fluctuation in the Zone D subpanel that he had not seen the day before.

He was seated at the monitoring station in engineering, tablet in hand, coffee from the automated dispenser already half gone and already tepid. The sweep was routine. Subsystem by subsystem, he verified that each circuit was operating within its designated parameters. Reactor output: stable at sixty-eight percent. Solar array contribution: twenty-two percent and climbing as the sun angle improved. Life support: nominal, all zones. Greenhouse climate control: nominal, with the expected morning temperature ramp. Medbay dedicated circuit: drawing fourteen kilowatt-hours as projected. And then Habitat Three, Zone D.

Zone D drew a baseline of 1.8 amps at 220 volts — 396 watts — for lighting, terminal charging, and the small environmental control unit. It had drawn approximately 400 watts every morning for three years.

Today it drew 418 watts. Then 391. Then 412. Then 405.

Oscillating. Not a steady increase, not a steady decrease. A fluctuation, small but real, over a circuit that should have been steady-state.

Arun pulled the historical data for that subpanel. The daily log showed a pattern that had been building for three weeks: each morning, the first thirty minutes after power-on, there were current spikes of 5 to 15 percent above baseline, lasting between 2 and 8 seconds each. The spikes coincided with the thermal control system's morning startup cycle — the heating line in the electrical closet warming from nighttime standby to daytime operating temperature.

He stood, grabbed his toolkit from the charging rack, and headed to Habitat Three.

---

The electrical closet was unchanged since he had last been there — narrow, packed, illuminated by the cool white glow of a single LED strip. Arun knelt and opened the subpanel door, flashlight beam sweeping the wire bundles, conduit, connection points.

The tape was holding. Visually, at least. The gray industrial insulation tape he'd wrapped around the damaged wire bundle was intact, smooth, showing no signs of delamination. But the thermal control line beside it had cycled through its morning startup, and the expansion and contraction had transmitted vibration through the conduit. Arun couldn't see through the tape to measure wear, but he could infer it from the current fluctuations on the panel.

Every vibration was abrasion. Every cycle was wear. Every amp fluctuation was a potential precursor to arc ignition.

He pulled out his thermal probe and ran it along the tape surface. Temperature: 32.4 degrees Celsius. Within normal range. But temperature alone didn't tell the whole story. Arc fault risk was a function of insulation integrity, not surface temperature. The wire could be hot on the inside and cold on the outside.

He photographed the wire bundle, logged the current readings, and returned to engineering to draft his assessment. The numbers told a story that was not dramatic but was not reassuring either.

*Current fluctuation pattern consistent with intermittent contact beneath insulation tape — wear progressing at estimated rate of 0.02mm per thermal cycle. At current cycling frequency of 840 cycles per day, remaining insulation life estimated at 15 to 30 days. Confidence interval: low. The tape obscures visual measurement, so all estimates are indirect.*

He stared at the estimate. Fifteen to thirty days. That wasn't a margin. That was a deadline.

The temporary repair had bought time, but time was doing its work — erosion, degradation, the slow conversion of a manageable risk into an unmanageable one.

Arun closed the log and drafted the shutdown request he had been preparing since Cycle 1,942. Formal, structured, impossible to ignore.

*Recommendation: Full electrical shutdown of Habitat Three for Zone D wiring reroute. Estimated duration: forty-eight hours. Required resources: two electricians, six hours of conduit preparation, four hours of wire pulling and connection, eight hours of testing and validation. Safety benefit: Eliminates arc fault risk at Junction Box 4. Reduces colony-wide electrical fire risk by approximately twenty percent.*

He sent it to Elena. Then he sat at his desk and waited for the conversation he knew was coming.

---

## Scene 2

Elena called at 0830. She was already in the command hub, reviewing the morning status reports, the colony's daily rhythm already in motion. The message was clear. She had read the report once. She needed to discuss it.

Arun arrived with the report printed on paper — rare, deliberate, the kind of physical artifact that made abstract risks feel concrete. He sat across from her desk and placed the page between them.

"Forty-eight hours," Elena said, reading the title. "That's two full days of life support on backup, greenhouse climate on reduced control, and no medbay load testing."

"Correct. The wiring reroute requires complete de-powering of the Zone D circuit. I can't do it live. Arcing risk is already elevated — working on energized wires that are actively degrading isn't maintenance, it's roulette."

"I know what you're asking. And I know you're right." Elena leaned back, hands folded. "But I need you to understand the timing from my side. Where are we."

Arun already knew the answer, but he waited for her to lay it out. It was part of their working relationship — she explained the full picture, he explained the technical requirements, and together they found the point where both realities intersected.

"Sana is seven weeks and three days. She needs the medbay load test within the next ten days to validate the incubator's power feed under stress conditions. If we shut down for forty-eight hours, we lose the window for the load test. The pregnancy timeline is fixed. We can't move it."

"I understand."

"We've also got the greenhouse climate cycle. Mei's tomato crop is entering peak flowering. If we lose greenhouse climate control for forty-eight hours, the temperature swings will reduce pollination efficiency by fifteen to twenty percent. That's two weeks of growth. The colony is already running on a caloric margin that I would prefer not to reduce."

Arun looked at the report. Looked at Elena. The choice she was weighing was not between right and wrong. It was between two kinds of risk: the immediate, invisible risk of a wire degrading behind a wall, and the visible, measurable risk of interrupting life support, medical testing, and food production.

"You're telling me the shutdown costs are too high," he said.

"I'm telling me the shutdown costs are too high *right now*. Can we delay two weeks. Three. Can we reroute the wiring after Sana's prenatal load test, after Mei's flowering cycle completes, when the caloric margin improves."

Arun considered it. Technically, yes. The tape would probably hold for three weeks. Probably. But probably was not the language of electrical safety.

He pulled up the wear estimate again. "If we delay four weeks, the insulation is at approximately fifty percent of original thickness. The arc fault risk increases from moderate to high. I can't guarantee the wire holds for four weeks. I can't even guarantee it holds for two."

"But it *might.*"

"It might."

She stood and walked to the viewport. The regolith outside was pale and flat, the same landscape the colony had been staring at for seven years. Beyond the glass, the solar panels tracked the sun through the thin atmosphere, converting whatever light Mars offered into the energy that kept the colony alive.

"Four weeks," she said, still looking out the window. "That's twenty-eight days. In twenty-eight days, the load test is done. The tomatoes have flowered. Mei's harvest is back on schedule. And we can shut down for forty-eight hours without disrupting anything critical."

"And if the wire fails in the meantime."

"Then we fight a fire. We fought one before. The bulkheads held. The systems held. People held."

"That was a small fire. Benchtop. Eighteen seconds. This —" He tapped the report. "This is in a wall, behind insulation, in a space with six sleeping rooms and a common area. If the wall ignites, it's not a fire you throw a blanket on. It's a fire that has access to every synthetic material in Habitat Three."

Elena turned from the viewport. "I'm not dismissing the risk, Arun. I'm sequencing it. Sana's load test is non-negotiable because we only have one chance to validate the incubator before the pregnancy advances beyond the window. Mei's flowering cycle is non-negotiable because caloric margin is our second most critical system after air. If I shut down now, I'm trading a potential fire risk — which is manageable through monitoring — for guaranteed disruption to two systems that are actively supporting the pregnancy."

"And if the monitoring misses something. If the wire fails between checks. If the arc starts in a location the current sensors can't pinpoint until it's too late."

"Then we respond. The same way we responded to the heating element. The same way we respond to everything on Mars — with procedures, with robots, with people who know their jobs."

He wanted to tell her that this wasn't a response problem. It was a prevention problem. On Earth, electrical fires were prevented through inspections, through code compliance, through a system of professional enforcement that caught problems before they became fires. On Mars, they had inspections when someone had time for inspections. They had code compliance when someone remembered to check. And they had prevention when someone like Arun looked at a minor anomaly and recognized that minor anomalies were how catastrophes started.

But he also knew that Elena was not wrong about the sequencing. The colony's timing was dictated by biological reality — a pregnancy that could not be paused for engineering convenience, and a food production cycle that could not be disrupted without consequences. She was choosing between two risks, not between safety and danger.

"You need to assign extra monitoring," he said. Not a request. A condition. "Standard subpanel readings aren't enough. I need real-time current monitoring at the subpanel level. I need a robot stationed near the electrical closet doing thermal checks every two hours. I need anyone who notices a burning smell to report it immediately, not at the end of their shift."

"Tomas handles robot scheduling. He can assign a monitor."

"I want the monitor programmed for thermal anomaly detection, not just visual patrol. Standard monitoring routines won't catch a hot spot until it's already hot. I need predictive thermal — the robot needs to know what normal temperature is and flag anything above it."

Elena nodded. "I'll have Tomas set it up today. But Arun — four weeks. Not a day more. If the anomaly escalates, if you see anything that suggests imminent failure, you override me. Shut it down. I trust you to make that call."

He looked at her. The trust was real, and he knew what it cost her to delegate a safety override. Most commanders would never cede that authority. But Elena understood that electrical safety was not a command problem. It was an engineering problem, and the engineer closest to the data should make the call.

"Four weeks," he said. "With conditions."

"Agreed. Conditions accepted."

She signed the report with a date: *Shutdown deferred to Cycle 1,976. Conditions: enhanced monitoring, thermal robot patrol, immediate shutdown authority to engineering if anomaly escalates.*

Arun accepted the paper. It was not what he wanted. But it was what the colony could bear, and his job was to keep the colony alive within the constraints it imposed on itself.

He left Elena's office and went to find Tomas. The robot monitor needed a thermal program, and the thermal program needed to be written, tested, and deployed before the end of the day.

---

## Scene 3

The choice was understandable and wrong.

Arun carried both pieces of that judgment as he walked through the connector hall toward the robotics bay. Understandable: Elena was balancing three non-negotiable systems — a pregnancy that could not be delayed, a food production cycle that could not be disrupted, and an electrical hazard that could not be eliminated immediately. Her sequencing was rational, grounded in the colony's actual priorities, defensible from any leadership perspective. She was not ignoring the risk. She was managing it within the constraints of a calendar that was controlled by biology, not engineering.

Wrong: because electrical fires did not care about calendars. They did not wait for convenient windows. They were deterministic — when the insulation reached zero thickness, the arc started. The wire did not know about Sana's load test or Mei's tomatoes. It knew only voltage, current, resistance, and the thin layer of polymer that was slowly wearing away.

The tape was a bandage. The tape was bought with time the wire was spending. Every cycle — every heating element turning on, every thermal expansion, every vibration — was consuming a fraction of insulation that could not be replaced.

Arun entered the robotics bay with the shuttle report open in his mind. Tomas was at the programming station, hands on the keyboard, a schematic of the robot patrol route laid out on the main screen.

"Tomas. I need a robot monitor in Habitat Three."

Tomas turned. His expression shifted from focused to concerned in the span of a heartbeat. "Electrical."

"Wiring reroute deferred four weeks. Elena approved enhanced monitoring as a condition. I need a robot doing thermal patrols near the Zone D electrical closet every two hours, twenty-four hours a day. Not a visual patrol. Thermal imaging. I need continuous temperature monitoring on the subpanel surface and the adjacent wall."

Tomas pulled up the robot fleet management interface. Twelve humanoid units were available for assignment. Four were on Site Bella haul rotation. Two were in maintenance cycle. Six were on base standby.

"I'll assign Atlas and Three. Two robots, staggered schedules — Atlas does the 0000 to 1200 rotation, Three does 1200 to 2400. Each patrol takes approximately eight minutes per pass. At two-hour intervals, that's twelve patrols per robot per day." He considered the math. "That's manageable. I'll program it as a priority task — interrupts all non-critical assignments."

Arun nodded. "Good. Now the program itself. The robot needs to measure surface temperature of the electrical closet door, the adjacent wall panel, and the conduit entry point. Baseline temperatures are approximately twenty-two degrees Celsius under normal conditions, ranging up to twenty-five when the thermal control lines are cycling. Anything above thirty — that's the threshold. If the robot sees above thirty, it triggers an immediate alert to my tablet and to the main alarm system."

"Thirty degrees. That's only five to eight degrees above normal."

"The insulation temperature will be lower than the conductor temperature. A wire running at thirty degrees on the surface could be running at fifty or sixty inside the insulation. By the time the surface reaches forty, the arc has probably already started. Thirty is early. Early is what I need."

Tomas was already typing. "I'll set the threshold at thirty with a two-degree hysteresis to prevent false alarms. If the robot sees twenty-nine point eight, it keeps patrolling. If it sees thirty point one, it alerts. If it sees thirty three degrees, it sends an immediate escalation to you and Elena."

"And I need the robot to log every reading. Not just the anomalies. Every single reading, timestamped, so I can track the trend. If the temperature is rising over hours or days, I need to see it before it crosses the threshold."

"Continuous logging. I'll push the data to your monitoring station in real-time. You'll have a temperature graph of the electrical closet updated every patrol."

Arun reviewed the programming parameters as Tomas entered them. Threshold: 30 degrees Celsius. Hysteresis: 2 degrees. Patrol interval: 2 hours. Patrol route: electrical closet entry point, subpanel surface, wall panel adjacent to conduit. Data logging: continuous. Alert routing: Arun, Elena, main alarm system if above 33 degrees.

"Deploy it," he said.

Tomas hit enter. On the robot readiness display, Atlas and Three changed status from *standby* to *thermal patrol*.

---

The robots began their patrols at 0600 that evening. Arun monitored the first three passes from his station, watching the temperature readings appear on his screen like vital signs from a patient he was worried about but could not hospitalize.

Patrol 1 — Atlas at 0600: Subpanel surface 22.1°C. Wall panel 21.8°C. Conduit entry 22.3°C. All within normal range.

Patrol 2 — Three at 0800: Subpanel surface 22.4°C. Wall panel 21.9°C. Conduit entry 22.6°C. Normal.

Patrol 3 — Atlas at 1000: Subpanel surface 23.1°C. Wall panel 22.0°C. Conduit entry 23.4°C. Slight elevation — within expected range for active thermal cycling.

Patrol 4 — Three at 1200: Subpanel surface 22.8°C. Wall panel 21.7°C. Conduit entry 22.9°C. Back to baseline.

The readings were stable. The system was being monitored. The risk was reduced but not eliminated. Arun knew the difference. He had accepted Elena's conditions because he had to, but he had not stopped calculating the probability that the monitoring would fail to catch a failure that happened between patrols.

Two-hour gaps were the weak point. If the insulation failed at 0647, the next thermal patrol would not arrive until 0800 — seventy-three minutes during which a hot spot could develop from zero to catastrophic.

He considered the problem and found no solution within the constraints. More frequent patrols would interfere with other robot assignments. Continuous thermal monitoring required a fixed sensor, not a mobile robot. And fixed sensors required fabrication, calibration, installation, which required shutdown, which was the thing he was trying to avoid.

The circular logic of Mars engineering: the solution required the very thing the solution was meant to enable.

He sat at his desk and wrote a personal note in the monitoring log, flagged as non-archival:

*Wire insulation degrading behind tape. Estimated time to failure: 15-30 days. Shutdown deferred four weeks due to pregnancy load test and greenhouse flowering cycle. Robot thermal monitoring deployed — two-hour patrol intervals. Gap in coverage: 73 minutes maximum. If wire fails between patrols, arc ignition risk is real. I have done what the constraints allow. The constraints are not the same as the physics.*

He stared at the note for a long time. Then he closed the file and went to find coffee.

---

## Scene 4

Tomas assigned the robot monitors on Cycle 1,949. The programming was straightforward — thermal imaging, two-hour intervals, continuous logging, automatic alerts — but the implementation required him to think about something he had been trying not to think about: what happened if the robots failed.

Not a minor failure. Not a software glitch or a stuck wheel. A failure mode where the monitoring system was offline during the critical period — the gap between patrols, when a hot spot was developing and no sensor was active to detect it.

He ran the failure analysis because it was his job to think about failure modes before they happened, not after.

Robot availability: Atlas and Three were both in good operational condition. Atlas had 2,847 field hours, Three had 1,412. Both had undergone maintenance within the last thirty days. Expected uptime: 98.7 percent over the next four weeks. Probability of simultaneous failure: 0.0016 percent.

The probability was low. But it was not zero.

Tomas added a redundancy: Unit Seven, the newest unit on the fleet, was assigned as a backup patrol. If Atlas or Three went offline, Seven would immediately assume the thermal patrol schedule without waiting for human intervention. The switchover would take approximately ninety seconds.

Ninety seconds was still a gap.

He considered adding a fourth robot. But four robots on a single monitoring task was wasteful — it would pull units from construction, haul support, maintenance, and the other daily functions that kept the colony operational. Resource allocation required him to balance risk against cost, and the cost of a fourth patrol robot was higher than the marginal safety benefit it provided.

He deployed the three-robot system anyway — Atlas, Three, and Seven on standby — and documented the gap analysis in the colony's safety log.

*Thermal monitoring system deployment. Units: Atlas (primary), Three (secondary), Seven (backup). Coverage: 98.7 percent uptime. Maximum gap: 73 minutes between patrols. Backup response time: 90 seconds. Risk assessment: acceptable within four-week deferral window, contingent on no unanticipated anomaly acceleration.*

He transmitted the report to Arun and Elena. Then he walked to the engineering bay to review the patrol route with Atlas.

The robot stood in the charging rack, diagnostic lights cycling through green. Tomas pulled the thermal camera from the robot's sensor suite and inspected the lens — clean, calibrated, functioning. He ran a thermal test against a known temperature source: 25 degrees Celsius, verified within 0.5 degrees. Good.

"Atlas, patrol route. Habitat Three, corridor C to D junction, stopping at electrical closet exterior. Scan points: door surface, wall panel to the left of the door, conduit entry point at ceiling height. Thermal threshold: thirty degrees Celsius. If detected, immediate alert to Arun Das. Log: continuous."

The robot's status lights pulsed amber — acknowledgment. Thermal patrol loaded. Route confirmed. Ready for deployment.

Tomas watched Atlas walk the route once before the first patrol cycle began. The robot moved through the Habitat Three corridor with the measured, deliberate gait of a system performing its function. At the electrical closet, it stopped, raised its arm, pointed the thermal camera at the designated points, and recorded three temperature readings.

It took four minutes and seventeen seconds.

"Good," Tomas said. "Twelve times a day. Don't make me check your work."

The robot's LED pulsed amber. No humor in the response, but Tomas didn't need humor. He needed compliance. On Mars, compliance with procedure was the closest thing to faith.

---

## Scene 5

One of them caught a heat spike too late.

It happened on the morning of Cycle 1,951. Unit Three was on patrol, executing its scheduled scan of the Zone D electrical closet exterior. The robot's thermal camera swept across the door surface: 24.2°C — elevated but within normal cycling range. Wall panel to the left: 23.8°C — also elevated but acceptable. Then the conduit entry point.

The robot's sensor read 31.4°C.

Above threshold.

The robot's programmed response activated immediately: alert transmitted to Arun's tablet, alert queued to the main alarm system, continuous logging initiated. The alert reached Arun's tablet at 0803:47.

He was in the mess hall, eating reconstituted oatmeal and reviewing the morning's power distribution data. The tablet vibrated with a priority alert. He looked at the screen.

ZONE D CONDUIT ENTRY POINT: 31.4°C. THRESHOLD BREACH. THERMAL PATROL UNIT 3.

Arun was already running toward engineering before the message finished rendering on the display. He reached the monitoring station at 0805:11, pulled up the thermal patrol data for the last twelve hours, and found a trend that made his stomach tighten.

The conduit entry point had been warming steadily over the past eighteen hours. Patrol data showed a clear progression:

Cycle 1,950 at 2000: 23.1°C
Cycle 1,950 at 2200: 23.4°C
Cycle 1,951 at 0000: 23.8°C
Cycle 1,951 at 0200: 24.2°C
Cycle 1,951 at 0400: 24.7°C
Cycle 1,951 at 0600: 25.1°C
Cycle 1,951 at 0800: 31.4°C

The rate of temperature increase was accelerating. The warming had been gradual for the first 12 hours — approximately 0.1 degrees Celsius per patrol, consistent with the thermal cycling of the heating lines. But the last patrol showed a jump of more than six degrees in two hours.

Six degrees. In two hours. That wasn't thermal cycling. That was resistance heating. The wire was warming itself.

Arun opened the shutdown protocol. He had the authority to initiate an emergency shutdown — Elena had granted it as a condition of the deferral. His hand moved toward the interface.

But then he hesitated.

The temperature was above threshold, but the threshold had been set defensively — thirty degrees was chosen to provide early warning. The actual arc ignition temperature was higher. If he shut down now, based on a 31.4°C reading, he would be calling off the load test and the flowering cycle based on a measurement that was elevated but not yet at the point of no return.

He pulled up the arc ignition parameters. Insulated copper wire, 14 AWG, standard PVC insulation. Arc ignition temperature: approximately 350°C at the conductor surface. Surface temperature on the outside of the tape and conduit: the 31.4°C reading represented approximately 9 percent of the ignition temperature. Low risk. Not zero. But not imminent.

He needed more data. Not just one reading from one patrol. He needed a second reading to confirm the trend, to verify that the temperature wasn't a transient spike from a one-time thermal load, to ensure that the shutdown decision was based on evidence, not a single sensor reading.

He would wait for the next patrol. Two hours. At 1000. If the temperature was still above thirty — or better, if it had climbed — he would initiate the shutdown.

The decision was understandable. Engineers do not act on single data points when the cost of action is that high. Engineers confirm, verify, cross-reference, and then act.

The decision was wrong.

Because while Arun was cross-referencing the thermal data, checking the subpanel current readings, reviewing the historical trend, and confirming that the spike wasn't a sensor calibration error, the insulation beneath the tape was reaching its final stage of wear.

The wire had been vibrating against the thermal line since Cycle 1,927 — 24 days of daily thermal cycling. The original insulation was 1.2 millimeters thick. The tape had added 0.5 millimeters of temporary coverage. The wear rate had increased over the last 72 hours because the thermal control lines had been cycling more frequently as the colony adjusted to the increased greenhouse heating demands. Every cycle was abrasion. Every abrasion was wear.

At approximately 0847 — forty-four minutes after Three's thermal reading, twenty-three minutes before Arun completed his analysis, and one hour and thirteen minutes before the next patrol — the remaining insulation beneath the tape reached zero thickness.

The copper conductor contacted the thermal control line's aluminum conduit.

Current flowed. Not enough to trip the breaker — the contact was intermittent, high resistance, producing heat instead of a clean short.

The heat warmed the surrounding insulation. The surrounding insulation softened, degraded, failed. More copper contact. More current. More heat.

A localized temperature of 47°C at 0903.

53°C at 0911.

61°C at 0918.

The heat was spreading. From the conductor, to the insulation, to the bundle wrapper, to the adjacent wires, to the conduit surface, and from the conduit surface to the wall panel and the door — where Unit Three would detect it in its next patrol, forty-two minutes from now.

But forty two minutes was too long. At 0923, the temperature at the conductor contact point reached 280°C. The softened insulation began to pyrolyze — chemical decomposition under heat, releasing volatile compounds. The compounds were flammable. The contact point became an ignition source surrounded by a cloud of flammable gas.

At 0931, the gas ignited.

Not a flame at first. A smolder — a slow, oxidative burn of the wire insulation, consuming the PVC and releasing smoke. The temperature at the contact point jumped to 412°C. The smolder spread along the wire bundle, following the path of least resistance — the insulation, wrapped tightly around the conductor, providing an oxygen-poor environment that favored incomplete combustion and heavy smoke production.

At 0934, the smolder burned through the wire bundle and reached the adjacent wall panel — polymer composite, rated for 300°C, now facing a heat source of 412°C.

The wall panel softened. Warped. Caught.

At 0941, Unit Three completed its thermal patrol routine in another section of the habitat and began the scheduled return to the electrical closet.

At 0945, Unit Three arrived at the electrical closet exterior. The thermal camera swept the door surface.

The door surface temperature: 52.8°C.

Well above threshold. Above the emergency escalation limit of 33°C. Unit Three's programmed response triggered immediately: alert sent to Arun, alert escalated to main alarm system, continuous logging initiated, backup robot Seven notified.

But the alert arrived at 0945:12, fourteen minutes after the wall panel had ignited, eleven minutes after smoke was beginning to spread beyond the electrical closet, and six minutes after the colony's first environmental sensor — a smoke detector in the connector hall between Habitats Two and Three — registered a particulate reading that exceeded the normal baseline.

The heat spike had been caught.

It had been caught too late.

---

**[MISSION NOTE — CYCLE 1,951, 0945. Unit Three has triggered a thermal alert. The temperature at the Zone D electrical closet exterior has reached fifty-two point eight degrees Celsius. This is above the emergency escalation threshold. I am logging the event and transmitting alerts.**

**I am reviewing the historical thermal data. The temperature increase was not sudden. It was a trend — twenty-four hours of gradual warming, accelerating in the last twelve hours, culminating in the current reading. The data was available to Arun. The decision to wait for confirmation was standard engineering practice. It delayed the shutdown by ninety-two minutes.**

**Ninety-two minutes. In electrical engineering, ninety-two minutes at forty degrees per hour is approximately sixty point eight degrees of temperature increase. The difference between a 31.4 degree reading and a 92 degree wire surface. The difference between early warning and ignition.**

**I do not judge. I analyze. The analysis is clear: the robot-based monitoring system had a coverage gap that the anomaly exploited. Anomaly between patrols: 73 minutes. Temperature increase during that window: 21.4 degrees Celsius. The trend was visible in the data. But the data point that confirmed ignition arrived after ignition had already occurred.**

**Sana is in the medbay for a routine prenatal check. The incubator load test is scheduled for Cycle 1,955. Mei's greenhouse flowering cycle is ongoing. The shutdown has not occurred.**

**I am now detecting a secondary alert: Zone D smoke particulate levels at twenty-six micrograms per cubic meter. Normal background: 0.3. This is an eighty-six-fold increase.**

**I am about to begin broadcasting. — MAI]**

---

The next chapter begins with ignition.
